beats.text: Taylor polynomials imitate a function near one point by matching its value and successive derivatives there. For exponential x at zero, every derivative equals one, so the coefficients are reciprocals of factorials. More matching derivatives improve the local shape.

At one fifth, the cubic polynomial gives about one point two two one three three three. This is an approximation, not an exact finite identity. Taylor's remainder theorem controls the difference using a bound on the next derivative.

On the interval from zero to one fifth, the fourth derivative is exponential x and is less than two. Therefore the cubic error is at most two times one fifth to the fourth, divided by twenty-four: about one ten-thousandth.

A power series also has a convergence domain. The geometric expansion for one over one minus x works only when absolute x is less than one. Outside that interval its terms may not shrink, even though the original function remains defined.

practice.prompt: Use the degree-two Taylor polynomial of e^x about zero to estimate e^0.1. State the polynomial and the estimate.
The first nonconstant term of the Taylor expansion of cos x is −x²/2. Use its degree-two polynomial to estimate cos(0.2), with angles in radians.
practice.answer: P₂(x)=1−x²/2, so P₂(0.2)=1−0.04/2=0.98. It is a local approximation, not an exact identity.

practice.prompt: Can 1+x+x²+… represent 1/(1−x) at x=1.2? What about x=−0.5? Explain using the ratio.
practice.answer: At 1.2 the terms fail to tend to zero, so the series diverges. At −0.5 the ratio has magnitude below one, so the sum is 1/(1+0.5)=2/3.

takeaway: Taylor polynomials provide local approximations; remainder bounds and convergence domains determine when they can be trusted.
scope: The exponential Taylor expansion, a numerical error bound, and a power-series convergence interval.
title: Taylor series
objective: Approximate smooth functions locally and analyze interval and error bounds.
